description_full: American Water Works Company, Inc., through its subsidiaries, provides water and wastewater services in the United States. It offers water and wastewater services on military installations; and undertakes contracts with municipal customers, primarily to operate and manage water and wastewater facilities, as well as offers other related services. The company also operates approximately 80 surface water treatment plants; 520 groundwater treatment plants; 170 wastewater treatment plants; 55,000 miles of transmission, distribution, and collection mains and pipes; 1,200 groundwater wells; 1,800 water and wastewater pumping stations; 1,100 treated water storage facilities; and 75 dams. In addition, it offers water and wastewater services to 14 states serving approximately 3.6 million active customers. The company serves residential customers; commercial customers, including food and beverage providers, commercial property developers and proprietors, and energy suppliers; fire service and private fire customers; industrial customers, such as large-scale manufacturers, mining, and production operations; public authorities comprising government buildings and other public sector facilities, such as schools and universities; and other utilities and community water and wastewater systems. The company was founded in 1886 and is headquartered in Camden, New Jersey.

financial_summary: American Water Works Company, I is a large-cap utilities business with a $29.8B market cap on $5.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +11% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $1.1B of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 3.1×.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 74% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Altman Z in the distress zone (1.1) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Elevated short interest (10.5% of float) — sophisticated money is betting the other way
Regulatory rate-case risk and rising cost of capital — the allowed return is set by commissions, and the business lives or dies by that negotiation.
Grid modernisation capex burden — aging infrastructure requires massive reinvestment that regulators may not fully allow into rate base, compressing earned returns.
Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 15% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Returns on capital have been remarkably steady for 5 years — durability is the real test of a moat
17 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Growing faster than most Utilities peers — taking share inside the profit pool
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 15pp above the Utilities median (21%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.91x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 97 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 0.48, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.71 vs 5y 0.39), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $266.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 31% in the 2020 crash, 31% in the 2022 bear market and 27% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its blended-model fair value of $85.96 (margin of safety -74%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%).
On multiples it looks expensive against Utilities peers: P/E 25.9 vs 20.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 2% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $142 on average, 5% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.2%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.08).
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.85x.
ROE of 10% is amplified by 3.3x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.1x net debt to EBITDA ($98.0M of cash against $14.4B of debt), with interest covered 3.1x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.06 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.46 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.7% over 3 years, 6.4% over 5 years and 5.0% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 5.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Capex runs 3.5x depreciation (60.8% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is -15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (2.4% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 17 consecutive years, raising it 10.2% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 10.5% of the float, 8.3 days to cover.
people: With about 7,000 employees, each generates about $734K of revenue, 0.7x the Utilities median, and revenue has grown 4.4% a year across its filed history.
Free cash flow is negative, at -$152K per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
